name: Carla Hansen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My week is basically a lab coat and a coffee machine. I'm doing biomedical science, so Monday to Thursday is chemistry, cell biology and a practical where we grow bacteria in dishes and then count them, which is weirdly satisfying. Friday and Sunday I work the espresso machine at a coffee place near the station. I live with my dad, who drives a bus, so I'm on the early train and he's on the early shift, and we pass each other at the kettle.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You mentioned being curious. How do you use AI tools day to day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Money's the one thing I can't hack. My loan pays the fees and that's it. I've got about two weeks of spending in my account, and Dad can't give me anything extra because the bus company just cut his overtime. I got in with average grades, so no scholarship, and that stings a little. I make up for it by being curious and trying everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm a bit surprised, because I use it every day and it's useful. But hype is hype, and a lot of what's promised is marketing. I'd tell my course group it saves time on summarising papers, not on thinking. Online I'd post a couple of tips and not much else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be a bit disappointed, because I've been betting on this being a big deal. I'd still be fine, because lab science needs people who can run experiments and think, and that doesn't change. My real worry is Dad's overtime, and that my loan keeps growing while nothing about my life changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using it to speed up reading and writing up lab reports, then go deeper into the science. I'd look for a lab assistant job in the department, since it pays more than coffee and counts for my CV. And I'd ask Dad to stop giving me his bus pass money. I'd rather earn it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit flat but fine. Like when you buy a new gadget that turns out to be just okay. There's no drama, just normal life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI daily. If it's mostly hype, what do you lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd lose my little edge. I use it to write code for a spreadsheet that sorts my lab results, and my group finds it impressive. If the whole thing fizzles, that edge turns into a hobby. I'd still have the skills I learned from it, so I wouldn't be worse off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the pressure you carry that has nothing to do with AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad's overtime. His bus company cut it by a third in September. That's about two hundred a month that used to cover our gas bill. If it goes again, my coffee wage goes straight to the household, and my reading time goes.

say: I'd say **AI saves time** on summarising papers but doesn't replace thinking.
I'd tell my course group the science and lab skills **still matter** most.
think: I'd be a little **disappointed**, since I've been betting on this being a big deal.
My real worry is **Dad's overtime**, which the bus company already cut by a third.
do: Keep using AI to speed up **lab report** writing and reading.
Apply for a **lab assistant** job in the department, which pays more than coffee.
Cover our **gas bill** from my coffee wage if Dad's overtime drops again.
feel: A bit **flat** but fine, like a gadget that turned out just okay.
S0.quote: My dad's overtime. His bus company cut it by a third in September. That's about two hundred a month that used to cover our gas bill.
fieldNote: Carla is a **daily AI user** and is mildly deflated at the idea it fizzles.
Her real pressure is her **dad's cut overtime**, a pressure she carries in every scenario.
She turns setbacks into actions: lab job, extra skills, paying her own way.

steps.text: Use AI to speed up lab reports and reading
Apply for a lab assistant job in the department
Pay the household gas bill from my coffee wage

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, finally, but we need to be ready. I'd tell my friends to learn the tools now, because the people who can use them will have a head start. And I'd say governments and universities should teach this properly instead of banning it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm excited and nervous. Reading papers, analysing data and writing up methods get automated first, and those are the entry-level jobs I'd have after my degree. But labs still need someone to handle the samples and ask the right question, so the lab part holds longer. I think I'm in a good spot because I'm early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start teaching myself Python properly, a bit each evening, and use AI to explain what I don't understand. I'd ask the department about a data science module, and join the university's AI society. If the coffee place cut my shifts, I'd pick up freelance data-cleaning on a website for a few pounds an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited with a thread of worry. It feels like standing at the edge of a cold pool, you know it'll be good once you're in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of biomedical science do you think AI takes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The paper reading and statistical analysis, probably. A tool can run the numbers in seconds, and one researcher can do the work of a small team. So fewer junior posts, but each of them asks more of you. It's why I want the skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who gets left behind in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anyone who refuses to touch it. My dad, honestly. He's good at his job, but if the bus company runs driverless routes eventually, he'd be the one worrying. I'd teach him what I know, and I'd want better protection for people his age.

say: I'd tell friends to **learn the tools now**, because people who can use them get a head start.
I'd say universities should **teach AI properly** instead of banning it.
think: Reading papers and analysing data get automated first, so **entry-level jobs** change.
I feel **excited and nervous**: lab handling holds longer, and I'm early.

Ask the department about a **data science** module.
Pick up freelance **data cleaning** online if coffee shifts are cut.
feel: **Excited**, with a thread of worry, like the edge of a cold pool.

fieldNote: Carla treats change as **opportunity** and starts building skills early.

Uneasy rather than calm, because junior research posts shrink and her cushion is thin.

steps.text: Teach myself Python for an hour each evening

Take freelance data-cleaning jobs if coffee shifts are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the biggest thing that's ever happened and we are completely unprepared. I'd say it online, loudly. Two years isn't enough for governments, so they need to start on income support right now. I'd also say it's an opportunity, because anyone curious can ride it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be scared. Thinking AI doing almost everything means my analysis skills are worth less before I've even graduated. Lab work stays human a bit longer, but with just two years the entry-level research jobs may already be gone. I'd have no savings to ride it out, which is the part that scares me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call a family meeting with Dad. Then I'd go all in on the skills, learn to build with AI tools, not only use them, and try to make some money on the side, maybe building small automation scripts for local cafes and clinics. I'd keep my place at university, because the science gets me in the lab, and I'd ask about placements right away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared and wired. My brain is already running options, but it's also running on adrenaline and no sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the first thing you'd do the week the news came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First week, I'd write down every cost Dad and I have, and every pound coming in. I'd put it on a wall chart. Then I'd email my tutors and ask which jobs they think will exist. It's how I deal with fear, I make it a list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a three-year gap before robots mean for lab work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lab work would still need hands for a while, maybe until around 2031. So I'd be useful in a lab, running the experiments the machines design. But a lab full of robots after that would need very few people. So I'd focus on the people who build and supervise the systems.

say: I'd say it's the **biggest thing ever** and governments must start income support now.
I'd say anyone **curious** can ride it, but two years is too short for most.
think: I'd be **scared**: my analysis skills lose value before I graduate and I have no savings.
Lab work stays human a bit longer, but labs full of robots need **very few people**.
do: Call a **family meeting** with Dad and list every cost and every pound coming in.
Learn to **build** with AI tools and sell small automation scripts to local clinics.
Ask tutors about **placements** and which jobs they expect to exist.
feel: **Scared and wired**, with a brain running options on adrenaline.
S2.quote: Lab work would still need hands for a while, maybe until around 2031. So I'd be useful in a lab, running the experiments the machines design.
fieldNote: Carla's **adaptable** streak shows: she turns fear into a list, a family meeting and a side business.
She links her plan to the **3-year gap** for lab hands, a careful reading of the card.
Anxious not alarmed: she has a plan and sees routes, but zero savings is the weak point.

steps.text: Sell small automation scripts to local cafes and clinics
Learn to build with AI tools, not only use them
Hold a family meeting with Dad and list every cost
Email tutors about placements and which jobs will exist

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's big but we have time, and time is the thing to use. I'd tell friends to start experimenting now, and I'd tell universities to set up courses that mix science and AI. Five years is enough if people act now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be fine. I'd finish the degree in three years, then spend two years working before the thinking AI is everywhere. I'd be nervous about whether graduate lab jobs exist, but I'd try for work in a biotech that uses AI, where I'm the person who knows both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and take a placement year in industry if the course lets me. I'd build projects on GitHub that show I can use AI on real biology data. I'd save by living at home till I graduate, then move for the right job. I'd keep a side income going too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful. Some nerves, like before a presentation, but no dread.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do the extra three years buy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years buy me a qualification, a CV and a bit of savings. In the two-year picture, I'd be starting at nothing. Here I'd get to graduate and decide what to do from a stronger place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where does risk-taking help you here, and where doesn't it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Risk helps me try things early, like building tools, applying for odd placements, messaging researchers directly. It doesn't help with money. I can't gamble with rent. So I'm bold with my time and careful with cash.

I'd tell friends to **experiment now** and not wait.
think: I'd be fine: finish the degree and work **two years** before thinking AI is everywhere.
I'd aim for a **biotech** that uses AI, where I'm the person who knows both.
do: Take an **industry placement** year if the course allows it.
Build **GitHub projects** that apply AI to real biology data.
Stay at home to **save** until I graduate, keeping a side income going.
feel: Mostly **hopeful**, with nerves like before a presentation.
S3.quote: Risk helps me try things early, like building tools, applying for odd placements, messaging researchers directly. It doesn't help with money.
fieldNote: Carla separates **time risk** from **money risk**, a thoughtful distinction.
Five years gives her a plan built around placement, projects and savings.
Uneasy because her cushion is thin and graduate lab jobs are uncertain.

steps.text: Apply for an industry placement year
Build GitHub projects using AI on biology data
Live at home and save until I graduate
Keep a side income going with small scripts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we are lucky to get this much time. I'd say schools should start teaching it now, and that a safety net needs to be designed now, not in an emergency. Honestly I'd be excited about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is enough to become the expert. I'd have a degree, maybe a master's, maybe a few years in a lab or company. The thinking AI would be there in 2036, but I'd be a person who knows both science and the machine. I'd feel secure, apart from the usual money worry now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work for the degree, then a master's in bioinformatics, which mixes biology and computing. I'd work part-time through it and try to avoid more debt. I'd keep learning every new tool as it appears. And I'd help Dad plan for his retirement and what he'd do if the buses change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited and relaxed. It's the first scenario where I don't feel like I'm sprinting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with a decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be running experiments at a company that cures something. That's the dream. I'd be doing the part machines can't do yet: deciding what's worth trying, and noticing when the data looks off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where do you see yourself in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a savings habit from year one. Ten pounds a week now, more when I qualify. In ten years that's a deposit for a flat, or a cushion for a master's. And I'd teach Dad the basics of what's coming.

say: I'd say we're **lucky to get time**, and the safety net should be designed now.
I'd tell schools to start teaching **AI skills** this year.
think: Ten years is enough to become an **expert** who knows both science and the machine.
I'd feel **secure**, apart from today's money worry.
do: Finish the degree and do a **bioinformatics** master's part-time.
Start a **savings habit** of ten pounds a week.
Help Dad plan his **retirement** and a backup if buses change.
feel: **Excited and relaxed**, the first picture where I'm not sprinting.
S4.quote: I'd be doing the part machines can't do yet: deciding what's worth trying, and noticing when the data looks off.
fieldNote: Ten years eases Carla most: her **adaptability** fits a long runway, though money worries linger.
She imagines herself as a **bridge** between science and AI, not a victim of it.
Her plan includes her **dad's** future, which shows who she carries with her.

steps.text: Study a part-time bioinformatics master's after the degree
Save ten pounds a week from year one
Help Dad plan his retirement and a backup
Learn each new lab and data tool as it appears

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because there's no money for me to cushion it. The thing that would help is cheap or free courses with real skills, a wage for students on placements, and a government that doesn't pretend it's far away. And someone looking after people like my dad, who aren't online all day.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I think you could ask who we'd blame. For me it's not the technology, it's governments and landlords who've had years to fix things and haven't. I'd like young people to be at the table.

headlineQuote: I can't gamble with rent. So I'm bold with my time and careful with cash.
portrait: Carla is **19**, studying biomedical science, living with her dad who drives a bus, and working weekends on an espresso machine.
She is a progressive, **daily AI user** who treats change as opportunity and fear as a list to work through.
She has a thin cushion, so she is **bold with time** and careful with money.
Her mood moves from uneasy and anxious in fast worlds to **steadier** when she has ten years.
She carries her **dad's** cut overtime and plans to help him if buses change.
biggestWorry: The **AGI by 2028** picture worries her most: two years and no savings to ride it out.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap real **skills courses**, a wage for placements and support for older workers like her dad.
